How to use the simulator

1 Quick start · 2 Top bar · 3 Tabs · 4 DCS console · 5 Faceplates · 6 Trends and alarms · 7 Heater EMS · 8 Field · 9 Exercises · 10 Debrief and export · 11 Symbols

1 · Quick start

  1. Click anywhere once so the browser allows alarm sound. The top bar should show 🔔 Sound on.
  2. The session opens lined out at design: 218.75 m³/h of light crude (33 000 barrels a day), heater outlet 388 °C, all five products on specification.
  3. Open P&ID to see the plant sheet by sheet, then DCS console to operate it. The display bar has the nine graphics 1–9 of the unit.
  4. Go to Exercises, pick Training, Think EQUIPPED or Procedures, and load one. A blue banner gives the situation; Acknowledge on the banner hides it.
  5. Click any instrument bubble, pump or switch on a graphic to open its faceplate on the right; change mode, set point or output there.
  6. Crude units are slow: use Speed 5×–20× and Freeze while you think. A cold start-up takes several simulated hours.
  7. When finished, open Debrief and grading for your score, then Data export to download CSV files for your report.

2 · Top bar

ControlWhat it does
ClockSimulated time since the session or exercise started.
Freeze / RunPauses and resumes the simulation; you can still read and click while frozen.
Speed1×, 2×, 5×, 10× or 20× real time. Grading uses simulated time.
Status lampGreen: heater firing. Amber: heater EMS idle or purging. Red: heater tripped. Click it to open the Heater EMS tab.
Sound / Silence / AcknowledgeSound on or off; Silence stops the horn until the next new alarm; Acknowledge accepts every alarm.
ScoreContinuous score out of 100 (see the Workbook, section 7).

4 · DCS console

The graphics follow the unit: 1 Overview, 2 Preheat overview (crude-side temperatures and a profile chart), 3 Preheat detail (every exchanger with crude and hot-side temperatures, duty now against design), 4 Desalters, 5 Heater, 6 Tower (with a tray-temperature profile), 7 Pump around (heat removal split), 8 Strippers (product quality table) and 9 Overhead (condensers, reflux drum, off-gas). Choosing a graphic also selects its trend group.

Instrument bubble anatomy: letters on top (FIC = flow indicating controller, TI = temperature indicator, AI = analyzer, LIC = level controller, PDI = differential pressure), loop number below, live value underneath. Controllers show their mode (MAN / AUTO / CAS) at the upper right. A value turns red while its tag is in alarm and flashes until acknowledged. Square frames are trip switches (FSL-105A/B). Pumps are green when running and red when stopped; block valves are green open, red closed; control valves show % open.

6 · Trends and alarms

Trends hold up to four hours at one point per second; choose the group, window (5–60 min) and pen colours. Selected tag shows PV, SP and OUT of the chosen controller. The alarm summary lists the newest unacknowledged alarm first; click a row to acknowledge and open that tag. Event alarms: EMS trip, low-flow trips bypassed, oil under-carry, relief valves lifting, boot overflow, wash zone dry, draw tray dry and high tube skin.

7 · Heater EMS

States IDLE → PURGING → PURGED → RUN. Purge needs both fuel EMS valves closed, FIC-106 and PIC-112 in MAN at 0 %, both passes above 40 m³/h (or HS-105A bypass) and no snuffing steam. Light on fuel gas only with FIC-106 in MAN at 3–15 %; a 10 s trial must prove flame. Fuel oil is admitted separately once PDC-111 shows atomising steam. Trips close both fuel valves and put TIC-101, FIC-106 and PIC-112 in MAN at 0 %. HS-105B is the emergency shutdown pushbutton.

8 · Field

Start and stop pumps (a tripped motor will not restart while its fault is active: use the spare), open and close block valves, set the steam bypass globe valves and the boot drain in %, and put snuffing steam into the firebox. Local gauges read the process directly and are the independent check when a transmitter is suspect. Laboratory samples report product qualities and salt in the desalted crude after 2 simulated minutes.

9 · Exercises

Training: 29 single-fault exercises starting from design. Think EQUIPPED: 12 cases with only a situation (the instructor holds the key). Procedures: cold start-up, normal shutdown, emergency shutdown, P-9A recovery and a 30-minute optimisation; steps tick automatically, "!" marks a step done out of order, some steps need Mark done. What-if: seven sets (tower bottom, top, tower, diesel stripper, AGO stripper, reflux drum, analyzers); predict each variable, then the model runs a hidden copy for 30 minutes. Trend matching, scrambles and the DCS reading sheet are graded into the Debrief.

10 · Debrief and export

The debrief shows the continuous score with each deduction, performance figures, exercise grades, fault recovery times and the event log (filter and copy). Data export writes CSV files (UTF-8) of the run data, a design-versus-now snapshot and the event log. On GitHub Pages the file downloads normally; in claude.ai the download prompt appears. Nothing is kept after the page is closed: export before you leave.

11 · Symbols and colours

Lines: crude and residue blue, pumparounds and hot oil magenta, products green, steam red, fuel gas orange, fuel oil brown, water cyan, vapour and gas olive, signals dashed. Bubble colours: blue flow/pressure controllers, red temperatures, purple levels, green analyzers, black indicators.

The process · atmospheric distillation of crude oil

1 Principles · 2 Block flow diagram · 3 Process description · 4 What each unit does · 5 Steady state: streams · 6 Steady state: units · 7 Balances · 8 Key relationships for the operator

1 · Principles of the process

What the unit does. Crude oil is a mixture of thousands of hydrocarbons boiling from below 0 °C to above 700 °C. The atmospheric crude unit separates it by boiling range into light ends (off-gas), naphtha, diesel, atmospheric gas oil (AGO) and atmospheric residue. No chemistry is intended: it is a physical separation by partial vaporisation and fractionation, run at just above atmospheric pressure. The residue goes on to the vacuum unit, which recovers the heavier gas oils without heating them above their cracking temperature.

  • The true boiling point (TBP) curve. The crude is described by the volume fraction that boils below each temperature. For the design light crude about 24 % boils below 193 °C (naphtha and lighter), 47 % below 343 °C and 52 % below 367 °C. The cut point between two products is the TBP temperature where one product ends and the next begins. The product yields follow directly from the cut points, so a yield change is a cut-point change.
  • Flash zone vaporisation. The heater raises the crude to about 388 °C. It enters the tower through the transfer line, where the pressure falls and part of it flashes (the temperature drops to about 371 °C). Everything that must leave as naphtha, diesel and AGO, plus a small overflash of about 3 % of the feed, has to be vapour here. At design the flash zone vaporises % of the crude. More heater outlet temperature, lower tower pressure or more stripping steam all raise this figure.
  • Why the outlet temperature is limited. Above about 370–400 °C the heaviest molecules start to crack thermally. They form gas and olefins, and coke builds up inside the heater tubes. Coke raises the tube-metal temperature and the pass pressure drop. The heater outlet (TIC-101, 388 °C) is therefore a compromise between lifting enough gas oil and keeping the coils clean. TSHH-1007 trips the heater at 410 °C.
  • Stripping steam. Steam injected below the flash zone and into the side strippers lowers the hydrocarbon partial pressure. Light material then boils off at a lower temperature. This recovers diesel from the residue and removes the light "tail" from diesel and AGO (it raises their 5 % and 10 % points and flash point). All the steam leaves overhead and condenses as sour water in the V-4 boot.
  • Fractionation needs reflux. The trays between two draws separate them only when liquid flows down against the rising vapour. That liquid, the internal reflux, comes from heat removal above: the top reflux (FIC-101) and the two pumparounds (MPA, BPA). The tower heat balance fixes how much heat must be removed. The top temperature controller (TIC-102) adjusts the top reflux to take out whatever the pumparounds leave. More pumparound duty means less top reflux, more heat recovered at a useful temperature, and less fractionation above the pumparound.
  • Heat integration. About % of the heat that takes the crude from storage to the heater outlet is recovered in 11 exchangers. The heat comes from the tower overhead, the products, the pumparounds and the vacuum-unit streams. The fired heater supplies the rest. Losing a pumparound or fouling an exchanger therefore shows up as more fuel burned and a lower heater inlet temperature (TI-1003).
  • Desalting. Crude carries brine. Its chlorides hydrolyse to HCl in the heater and corrode the overhead, and its salts foul exchangers and poison catalysts downstream. Wash water (about 2.7 vol % of the crude) is mixed in and the emulsion is broken in an electric field. The salt leaves with the brine. The desalters run at 1034 kPa g, well above the vapour pressure of water and light ends at 150 °C, so nothing boils in the vessel.
  • Pressure. The tower runs as low as the overhead system allows (48 kPa g at the top, 13.8 kPa g in the reflux drum). A higher pressure means less vaporisation at the same temperature (heavier residue, lighter products) and more fuel to reach the same lift.

2 · Block flow diagram

Numbers in the flags refer to the stream table in section 5. Blue = crude and residue, green = products, magenta = pumparounds and vacuum-unit hot streams, brown = vapour and gas, red = steam, orange = fuel, teal = water. Dashed boxes list the hot side of each preheat exchanger.

3 · Process description

Crude charge and cold preheat (PID-001). Crude at about 53 °C is pumped from storage by P-1A/B at 218.75 m³/h (FIC-114, the feed master). Most of it passes through E-1, which condenses part of the tower overhead vapour. FCV-129 takes the flow that PIC-108 asks for, and FCV-130 bypasses about 10 m³/h round E-1. The crude then picks up heat from HVGO product in E-3, from diesel product in E-2 and from AGO product in E-14. It reaches the desalters at about 155 °C (TI-180).

Desalting (PID-002). FIC-132 splits the crude between two parallel desalters, V-3 and S-1. Wash water (FIC-103, FIC-133, 2.9 m³/h each, pumped by P-11A/B and warmed in E-13/E-19) is injected ahead of each vessel. The brine settles to an interface held at 15 % by LIC-103 and LIC-161 and leaves for treatment. PIC-108 holds the desalter outlet at 1034 kPa g by setting how much crude FCV-129 admits to the train. BV-102 bypasses both desalters in an emergency.

Hot preheat (PID-003). The desalted crude (about 149 °C) is boosted by P-2A/B to about 1940 kPa g and heated further:

  • E-15: HVGO reflux from the vacuum unit.
  • E-4: the mid pumparound (MPA).
  • E-5, then E-7: the bottom pumparound (BPA). The BPA goes through E-7 first, then E-5.
  • E-6: the vacuum-unit HVGO pumparound.
  • E-8 // E-18: vacuum residue. FIC-136 splits the crude over the pair and FIC-138 splits the residue.

The crude reaches the heater at about 276 °C (TI-1003).

Heater H-1 (PID-004). FIC-105A/B divide the crude equally between two radiant passes. FIC-114 is their master, so the passes follow the feed. The crude leaves at 388 °C (TIC-101) with part of it already vaporised. Fuel oil is the base load (PIC-112 at 689 kPa g, atomised with steam by PDC-111). Fuel gas (FIC-106) is the swing fuel chosen by HS-101 that TIC-101 moves. The heater EMS (UY-105) closes the fuel shutdown valves on these trips:

  • low pass flow (FSL-105A/B, 40 m³/h)
  • high-high coil outlet (TSHH-1007, 410 °C)
  • flame failure
  • manual ESD (HS-105B)

Crude tower V-1 (PID-005). The partly vaporised feed enters the flash zone below tray 4 at about 371 °C and 76 kPa g. The liquid falls to the bottom, where 3810 kg/h of stripping steam (FIC-109) recovers light material. The atmospheric residue leaves through P-3A/B to the vacuum unit (FIC-1102 in cascade from the bottoms level LIC-107). The vapour rises through 30 trays:

  • AGO is drawn from tray 12 (HCV-102).
  • The bottom pumparound is drawn from tray 9 and returns to tray 11.
  • The mid pumparound is drawn from tray 17 and returns to tray 19.
  • Diesel is drawn from tray 20 (HCV-101).
  • Top reflux returns to tray 30.

TIC-102 holds the top at 136 °C by setting the reflux (FIC-101).

Pumparounds (PID-006). P-9A/B circulate 87.5 m³/h of MPA through E-4 (FIC-104). P-10 circulates 99.6 m³/h of BPA through E-7 and E-5 (FIC-108). Together they remove about 7.9 MW from the middle of the tower and return it to the crude.

Side strippers (PID-007). Diesel and AGO flow by gravity into the strippers V-2A and V-2B. There, steam (FIC-111, FIC-112) strips the light ends back to the tower (trays 22 and 14). The stripper levels (LIC-108, LIC-109) set the product rates:

  • FIC-102: diesel by P-8A/B, cooled in E-2, E-11 and E-12.
  • FIC-113: AGO by P-7A/B, cooled in E-14.

On-line analyzers read the diesel 5 % and 90 % points (AI-103, AI-102) and the AGO 10 % point (AI-104).

Overhead (PID-008). The overhead vapour, naphtha plus all the steam, is condensed in E-1 (against crude), the air cooler E-9 (fan pitch HIC-100) and the water-cooled trim E-10. It is collected in the reflux drum V-4 at about 46 °C. The streams leave V-4 as follows:

  • Reflux: P-5A/B.
  • Unstabilised naphtha to the debutanizer: P-6A/B, FIC-100 in cascade from the drum level LIC-101. AI-100 and AI-101 read its IBP and end point.
  • Sour water from the boot: P-4 under LIC-102.
  • Uncondensed light ends: off-gas to the compressor.

PIC-102 holds the drum at 13.8 kPa g with a split-range scheme: natural gas in, then compressor spillback, then flare.

Utilities and safety. The unit uses:

  • stripping and atomising steam
  • fuel gas and fuel oil
  • cooling water for E-10 and E-12
  • electricity for pumps and fans
  • natural gas for drum pressure
  • the flare

The main hazards and their protections:

  • Loss of flow through a heater pass while firing: the coil overheats and cokes. The low-flow trip protects it.
  • A heater tube leak means a firebox fire: ESD, snuffing steam, isolate the passes.
  • Water reaching a hot tower flashes violently and damages trays. Check the boot level and never admit wet crude to a hot tower.
  • Overpressure of the desalters (PSV-108) and the drum (PSV-102).

Trainee workbook · Atmospheric Crude Unit Ver 1

Work through Parts A to G in order and keep your evidence (screenshots, CSV files) for the report.

1 Purpose · 2 The unit · 3 Control scheme · 4 Safety systems · 5 Operating rules · 6 Activities A–G · 7 Grading · 8 Report checklist

1 · Purpose

This workbook trains you to operate, monitor and troubleshoot the atmospheric section of a crude distillation unit: preheat train, desalters, two-pass fired heater, 30-tray crude tower with two pumparounds, diesel and AGO side strippers, and the overhead system. By the end you should be able to:

  1. Read the P&ID sheets and the nine DCS graphics, and state the normal value and alarm limits of every key tag.
  2. Explain how heat input, pressure, stripping steam, reflux, pumparounds and draw rates set the yield and quality of each product, and predict the direction every key variable moves after a change.
  3. Start the unit from cold through the heater EMS, line it out at design and bring every product on specification.
  4. Recognise equipment, instrument and process faults from alarms, trends and local checks, make the unit safe, and find the root cause with a systematic six-stage method.
  5. Improve the operation (yield, energy, flaring) and support your case with exported data.

2 · The unit

Crude from storage is pumped by P-1A/B through the overhead exchanger E-1 (FIC-129, with bypass FIC-130), E-3 (HVGO product), E-2 (diesel product) and E-14 (AGO product) to the two parallel desalters V-3 and S-1 (FIC-132 split, wash water by P-11A/B, brine on interface control). The booster pumps P-2A/B send it on through E-15 (HVGO reflux), E-4 (mid pumparound), E-5 and E-7 (bottom pumparound), E-6 (HVGO from the vacuum tower) and the parallel vacuum-residue exchangers E-8/E-18 to the two passes of heater H-1. Partly vaporised crude enters the flash zone of V-1 below tray 5. Four stripping trays below the flash zone use steam FIC-109. Diesel is drawn from tray 20 and AGO from tray 12 to their steam strippers V-2A and V-2B; the mid pumparound runs from tray 17 back to tray 19, the bottom pumparound from tray 9 back to tray 11. Overhead vapour is condensed in E-1, the fin-fan E-9 and the trim cooler E-10 into reflux drum V-4, which separates off-gas (to the compressor), naphtha (reflux and product) and sour water (boot, P-4). Residue goes to the vacuum unit.

Values are the model's lined-out design point. Rebasing and assumptions: SI units throughout; the vacuum-unit hot streams, the crude TBP curves, the heater efficiency (about 55 % of the fired heat reaches the crude) and a few preheat temperatures were set by balance where the source gave none.

3 · Control scheme

Key ideas: the crude rate is set by FIC-114 through the heater pass flows, and the desalter pressure PIC-108 pulls the matching crude through E-1. The heater outlet TIC-101 moves only the swing fuel. The top temperature sets how much naphtha goes overhead; the reflux is simply what the heat balance needs to hold it, so anything that removes less heat lower down (a pumparound, a fouled exchanger) shows up as more reflux. The draw valves set the diesel and AGO yields; everything not drawn off goes to the residue.

4 · Safety systems

Heater EMS: IDLE → PURGING → PURGED → RUN. Any trip closes the fuel gas and fuel oil EMS valves and puts the firing controllers in MAN at zero; the first cause is latched. Reset, purge and relight on gas every time.

Alarm limits

5 · Operating rules

  1. Never let water reach a hot tower. During start-up hold the heater outlet at 121 °C until water stops arriving in the V-4 boot, and never let the boot overflow.
  2. Keep the desalters liquid-full and above the bubble point (PIC-108 about 1034 kPa). Watch the interface: too low sends oil to water treatment, too high sends water with the crude.
  3. Protect the heater coils: both passes must flow before firing; a pass that loses flow overheats in seconds. Do not bypass the low-flow trips (HS-105A) except as the procedure says.
  4. Change one thing at a time and let the tower settle (10–20 minutes) before judging the result.
  5. Draw rate moves the heavy end, stripping steam moves the light end. Adjust the product and its neighbour together.
  6. Do not over-draw: if the draw trays run dry the overflash is lost and the wash zone cokes.
  7. Keep the drum pressure just above atmospheric (13.8 kPa g) and flaring to a minimum.
  8. Check two instruments before you believe one: TIC-101 against TI-1007A/B, FIC-114 against the pass flows and the local FG-114, PIC-108 against PG-108, FIC-101 against the local reflux gauge, LIC-107 against the sight glass.

6 · Activities

Part A · Familiarisation (about 30 min)

  1. On the P&ID sheets trace crude, residue, pumparound, product, steam, fuel and overhead paths; list every controller and what it moves.
  2. Visit all nine graphics and note the design value of each bubble.
  3. Complete the DCS reading sheet (Exercises): value, low and high alarm for 23 tags. Graded out of 15.

Part B · What-if predictions (about 45 min)

Work through the seven what-if sets. Predict ↑ / ↓ / — for every variable before checking, then explain each wrong prediction with a heat, material or pressure balance.

Part C · Cold start-up (graded)

    Part D · Training exercises

    Load each exercise from design. Record the first alarm and its time, the first variable you noticed, what you did, and the recovery time from the Debrief.

    Part E · Think EQUIPPED troubleshooting

    Each case gives only a situation. Work through the six stages; think of Equipment, Utilities, Instruments, Process, People, Environment and Downstream/upstream when you list causes.

    StageWhat you must produce
    1 EngageIs it an emergency? Keep running, reduce rate or shut down, and why.
    2 DefineProblem statement (what, where, when, how much), IS / IS NOT table, measurable target.
    3 ExploreRelevant balances, consistency checks between instruments and local gauges, recent changes, trends.
    4 PlanAt least three hypotheses, each with a diagnostic check (tag, tab, expected result), ordered by safety, time and cost.
    5 Do itRun the checks, name the root cause, apply the fix, predicting each response first.

    Part F · Trend matching and scrambles

    Match four unlabelled trend sets to their events and justify each from the six pens; put the scramble steps in order.

    Part G · Shutdown, optimisation and report

    Complete the normal shutdown and the diesel optimisation. For your start-up and one Part E case, download the run data (10 s interval) and the event log; plot the key variables against time and explain what happened.

          Design of the unit operation · atmospheric crude distillation

          1 · Fundamentals: the balances that size a crude unit

          A crude unit is designed around four balances, applied in this order: the TBP yield balance (what the crude can give), the flash-zone vaporisation (what must be vapour when the feed enters the tower), the heater duty (the heat needed to get there) and the tower heat balance (where that heat must leave again).

          1.1 TBP curve, cut points and yields

          The yield of each product is the volume fraction of the crude that boils between its two cut points: y = V(Tend) − V(Tstart). The model reads V(T) from the TBP curve of the crude (light, or blended with heavy).

              Assumptions and limits

                Operating windows · where the crude unit can run

                Every number comes from the simulator's own model (engine of this page) run offline as a private copy at design — never the running simulator. Grids were precomputed with the same engine (tools/compute.js); the point check runs the model live. Limits that the model does not hold are labelled assumed.

                1 Operability · 2 CV, MV, DV · 3 Variability · 4 Bounds · 5 Point check · 6 Capacity and turndown · 7 Type I · 8 Type II/III · 9 Monte Carlo · 10 n vs m · 11 Limitations

                1 · Operability: what an operating window is

                Operability is the ability of the unit to stay inside its bounds — safety, equipment, product quality, environment — while the inputs vary, without retuning or rebuilding it. The operating window is the set of conditions where every bound is met. It is found by stacking four things: how much the inputs vary, the bounds, the capacity of each piece of equipment, and the flexibility (the spare range of the handles) that can absorb the variation.

                Three ways of drawing a window are used below. Type I: valve outputs held, see which CV values result (the controllers are open). Type II: the control system as designed holds its set points; ask where a valve saturates or an uncontrolled variable breaks a bound. Type III: Type II repeated over the range of a disturbance (here crude type, ambient and crude temperature).

                2 · Controlled, manipulated and disturbance variables

                3 · The five sources of variability (design-basis memorandum)

                4 · Bounds: limits, design value, now and margin

                Each bound is [id, label, source, kind, value, low, high] in the engine (OW_B, ). Kinds: capacity (a valve outside 5–95 %, the compressor full, the heater rating, flooding ΔP), hard (trip settings, PSV sets, tube skin), product spec (analyser bands), alarm (the alarm table), CV held by a loop (alarm on a controlled variable: breaks only when its loop has run out of valve). Margin now ÷ design = (distance to the nearest limit now) ÷ (the same at design): 1 = as designed, 0 = on the limit, negative = outside. Now = the running simulator.

                Move the disturbances (or pick a preset) and run the model to steady state. The run starts from the design snapshot, applies the disturbances, moves the trip settings out of reach so the limit can be seen instead of a trip (restored afterwards), and checks every bound. Handle mode R moves what an operator would move with the charge (diesel and AGO draws, fuel-oil base load, pumparounds and stripping steam in ratio to charge); mode II leaves them at design.

                Press a preset or “Run this point”.

                6 · Capacity and turndown: the unit as a series plant

                Crude passes through pumps, exchangers, heater, column and overhead in series, so the unit can only take the charge that every element allows. Each bar is the range of crude charge a bound allows along a sweep from 80 to 260 m³/h (5 m³/h steps, all other disturbances at design); the green band is where all bars overlap = the window along the charge, and its ends give the turndown.

                10 · How many handles (n vs m) and which MV for which CV

                11 · Limitations

                • Steady state only: a point inside the window can still trip on the way there (fast disturbances, a pump trip). Transition operation covers the dynamics.
                • The model is lumped: the tower is a cut-point machine with a ΔP-based flooding check and no tray weeping, so the low end of the column is represented by the reflux and naphtha low-flow alarms, not by tray hydraulics.
                • Assumed limits: tube skin °C and a heater rating of % of the design fired duty; typical rangeabilities in the turndown table. Change them and the top and bottom of the window move.
                • Mode R is an idealisation of good operation (draws, base fuel, pumparounds and steam moved in proportion to the charge). Real operators move them in steps and with lags.
                • Runs use a 2 s integration step for 60 min from the design snapshot (the page's simulator uses 0.25 s); the end states agree to about 0.05 °C, checked in the node tests. Grid values between points are interpolated.
                • Alarm limits were set for design rates; several of them (reflux, naphtha, preheat temperatures) narrow the window at low charge or heavy crude. Whether they are true limits or alarms to re-range at turndown is an engineering decision.

                Flexibility · the handles that absorb variability

                Numbers are model runs with the Operating-windows engine (a private copy of the simulator at design, never the running one) or the model's own equations; anything else is labelled illustration or assumed.

                1 What it is · 2 Register · 3 How many · 4 Where: gains and interaction · 5 Fluid flow · 6 Heat transfer · 7 Production rate · 8 How much · 9 Recommendations

                1 · What flexibility is

                Flexibility is the ability to move the unit to a new operating point, or keep it at the old one when a disturbance arrives, by using handles that were designed in for that purpose. Three kinds are built into a crude unit: spare capacity (pumps, valves and the heater sized above the design flow), utility flows (fuel, pumparound duty, stripping steam, air-cooler pitch that can be turned up or down) and bypasses and splits (a stream sent round or shared between exchangers). Each costs money at design, so each must be justified by a disturbance in the design basis (see Operating windows).

                2 · Register of handles

                3 · How many handles

                4 · Where the handles act: gains and interaction

                Three cases decide whether two handles give two independent targets: independent (each handle moves only its own CV), spring (a handle also drags the other CV, but the pair can still be set), beam (both handles move the CVs in the same proportion, so the pair is really one handle).

                +5 % open-loop gain table

                6 · Heat transfer: Q = UA·ΔT and the bypass cases in this preheat train

                The three bypass arrangements of the lecture, as they appear here: (a) cold-side bypass — FCV-130 sends part of the crude round E-1, so E-1 heats less crude and the overhead leaves E-1 hotter; (b) hot-side split — FV-138 shares the vacuum residue between E-8 and E-18; (c) parallel cold-side split — FV-136 shares the crude between E-8 and E-18. A bypass only gives flexibility while the exchanger has surplus area: duty can be taken away by bypassing, never added beyond UA·ΔT.

                        9 · Step test and FOPDT model

                        Put the loop in MAN, step its output, and record the measurement. A first-order-plus-dead-time (FOPDT) model, K·e−θs/(τs + 1), is fitted by the two-point method: t28 and t63 are the times to reach 28.3 % and 63.2 % of the final change, τ = 1.5 (t63 − t28), θ = t63 − τ. A level is an integrator: the fit is a slope instead.

                        HAZID · hazard identification of the atmospheric crude unit

                        A plant-level, checklist-driven search for the major hazards of the unit, done on the PFD before the detailed HAZOP. Teaching study, Rev 0 · Issued for teaching: the risk matrix is an example and the ranking is the study team's judgement, not a design figure.

                        1 What HAZID is · 2 Method · 3 PFD and study areas · 4 Guideword checklist · 5 Hazard register · 6 Major accident hazards · 7 From HAZID to HAZOP and other studies

                        1 · What HAZID is and where it sits

                        A HAZID is a brainstorm held early (concept or FEED stage) on the PFD and plot plan. The team walks through the plant area by area and asks a fixed list of guideword questions, so that no class of hazard is forgotten. It finds the major accident hazards (MAH) and decides which of them need a detailed study. The HAZOP that follows works line by line on the P&ID.

                        2 · Method

                        1. Scope: the ACU from crude battery limit to the product, off-gas and residue battery limits, with its utilities.
                        2. Areas: the PFD is split into eight areas A1 – A8 (part 3).
                        3. Guideword checklist: for every area the team asks the 12 categories of part 4.
                        4. Existing controls, split as in a bow-tie: prevention (stops the event: control loops, alarms, trips, procedures) and mitigation (limits the consequence: relief, fire water, ESD, emergency response).
                        5. Rank each hazard with the shared 5 × 5 matrix: S is the worst credible severity with no credit for safeguards, L the likelihood with the existing safeguards, R = S × L. Hazards with S ≥ 4 that can kill or cause a major fire are flagged MAH.
                        6. Actions and further studies: each MAH is sent to the HAZOP, LOPA, consequence analysis or another study (part 7).

                            Safety layers · protection of the atmospheric crude unit

                            The safety hierarchy applied to this unit: process design → BPCS → alarms and operator → SIS → relief → containment → emergency response. Every layer is drawn on a dedicated P&ID of the safety-relevant core (heater H-1 and its fuel trains, the transfer line, V-1 bottoms, V-4 and the desalters). Settings come from the simulator model; items drawn dashed are recommended additions, not on the ACU P&ID set; limits marked "assumed" are not in the design data.

                            3 · What each layer does

                            4 · Integrity operating window

                            An integrity operating window (IOW) is the set of limits within which the equipment keeps its integrity. Inside the alarm limits the BPCS holds the unit (safe); between the alarm and the trip or relief setting the operator has limited time (a sustained excursion damages equipment); beyond the critical limit damage or loss of containment is expected. The arrow is the live value. Critical limits that are not in the design data are marked assumed.

                            A · Reliability for safety

                            A1 · Terms, with examples from this unit

                            A2 · Population lab: 100 bulbs from a Weibull distribution

                            Each bulb has a life ti = α(−ln(1 − (i − 0.5)/100))1/β; the bulbs are shuffled with a fixed seed so the picture is stable. At time t, Ns bulbs survive and Nf have failed. Over the next Δt = α/10 another ΔNf fail, so the failure rate is λ = ΔNf / (Ns Δt).

                            Population

                            A3 · PFD and proof testing

                            A safety device that fails dangerously stays failed until a proof test finds it. With a constant rate λ the probability it has failed by time t is 1 − e−λt; a test every T years resets it, giving a saw-tooth. The average over one interval is PFDavg = 1 − (1 − e−λT)/(λT) ≈ λT/2 when λT ≪ 1.

                            Device

                            A4 · Reliability block diagrams

                            A5 · SIF calculator

                            A SIF is a chain: sensor → logic solver → final elements. The chain fails if any subsystem fails, so the PFDs add. Pick a trip of this heater, change the voting, λDU or the test interval, and see where the PFD comes from.

                            A6 · Course parallel method

                            For branches in parallel with exponential lives, MTTFsys = Σ 1/λi − Σ 1/(λi + λj) + Σ 1/(λi + λj + λk) − …, and λsys = 1/MTTFsys.

                            Branches

                            A7 · Failure data used in this tab

                            B · Layer of protection analysis

                            B1 · The chain from cause to consequence

                            f(consequence) = IEF × P(enabling) × Π PFD(IPL) × Π CM RRF = f / f(target) (RRF ≤ 1: tolerable)

                            B2 · Five steps

                            1. Pick one cause–consequence pair from the HAZOP (a scenario) and rate the consequence severity.
                            2. Find each initiating event and its frequency; add any enabling condition.
                            3. List the safeguards and keep only those that are independent protection layers for that cause.
                            4. Multiply: IEF × enabling × PFDs × conditional modifiers, and add the causes.
                            5. Compare with the target for that severity. If RRF > 1, recommend a layer with PFD ≤ 1/RRF and size it (SIL).

                            B3 · Lecture example

                            B4 · Course criteria and risk matrix

                            Likelihood comes from the mitigated frequency; band edges lie halfway between decades (10−0.5, 10−1.5 …). Risk = S × L: 1 negligible · 2–6 low · 8–12 medium · 15–20 high · 25 extreme.

                            This matrix is stricter than the HAZOP tab's ranking (there 5–9 is medium and 10–16 high): LOPA judges against a target frequency, not a band.

                            1 · Where the SRS sits in the safety life cycle

                            IEC 61511-1 clause 10 asks for a written specification of every safety instrumented function before it is designed: what it protects against, what it measures, at what set point, how fast it must act, what the safe state is, how reliable it must be (SIL from the LOPA) and how it is tested, bypassed and reset. Design, testing and operation are then checked against it.

                            3 · Requirements of each SIF

                            Process safety time (PST) from the model: load the design state into a private copy, disable every trip, apply the demand, and log every 0.25 s until the hazard criterion. PST = time of the hazard − time the trip point is crossed. A second run with the trips live (plus 0.75 s sensor + logic before the valves move) shows whether the SIF actually stops the hazard. Hazard limits are assumed; see the notes in each card.

                            1 · Why incidents, and how to read a case

                            Almost every accident below had been foreseen by somebody: an inspection recommendation not carried out, a trip bypassed, a valve known to pass. Reading them is the cheapest way to learn what a HAZOP or a LOPA misses. Read each case in three steps:

                            1. What happened — the sequence, in the order the investigators established it.
                            2. Why — the immediate cause (the leak, the overfill, the flame-out) and the barriers that failed or were missing: the six layers of protection (L1 control … L6 emergency response, as in the Safety layers tab) and the management-system elements around them (MOC, hazard study, inspection, procedures, permits, siting, culture).
                            3. So what for the ACU — the same weakness on this unit, named by its tags and lines.

                            Think of the Swiss-cheese model: each layer has holes, and an accident needs the holes to line up. The point is to close holes in our own layers, not to blame the people who were there; most of them were doing what the system around them made normal.

                            Transition operation · atmospheric crude unit

                            Rev 0 · Issued for teaching. A transition is any time the unit moves between operating states: startup, shutdown, a rate change, a crude switch, regeneration or a by-passed item. Most incidents and most off-spec product happen in transitions, not at steady state. Every number below comes from scripted runs of this OTS model on an offline copy (the running simulator is never touched), or is labelled assumed.

                            1 Kinds · 2 Before startup · 3 Startup and shutdown steps · 4 Startup and shutdown runs · 5 Load following · 6 Crude switch · 7 Storage sizing · 8 Regeneration · 9 Limitations
                            Key lessons from the model
                            • Never step the heater outlet set point on a cold startup: the step trips TSHH-1007; ramps of 1–5 °C/min line out without a trip (§4a).
                            • Hold at about 121 °C until the tower is dry, or the water flashes and damages trays (§4a).
                            • Fuel out first, flow out last: stopping the pass flow while firing sends the tube metal far above its design value (§4d).
                            • Move the draws, pumparounds, steam and fuel oil with the rate; a crude switch needs new draw settings, and a slow blend only buys time (§5, §6).
                            • Control the result (COT), not a sum of demands (§5).

                            1 · Kinds of transitions in this unit

                            2 · Before startup, and the equipment transitions need

                            A unit designed only for steady state cannot start up. These items exist only for transitions:

                            3 · Startup and shutdown: step, why this order, safety concern

                            Steps are the unit's startup and shutdown procedures (graded practice in the Exercises tab). "Model run, min" is when the scripted run in §4 started each step.

                            Cold startup

                            4 · Scripted model runs: startup and shutdown

                            4a · Warm-up: set point stepped or ramped

                            Cold, empty unit; the steps of the startup procedure scripted in order up to light-off, then TIC-101 in AUTO at 121 °C and the set point raised to 388 °C in different ways. Residue circulates through both passes at about 55 m³/h each.

                            4b · The full cold startup

                            4c · Normal shutdown

                            4d · Order of steps at the heater: fuel first or flow first?

                            From design rate. The firebox keeps radiating for about a minute after the fuel stops (model lag), so whatever flow is in the coils then decides the tube temperature.

                            Fuel first with the crude kept flowing leaves the coils at their running temperature. The emergency shutdown for a tube leak stops the pass flow together with the fuel on purpose (it stops feeding crude into the fire), and pays for it with a short tube-metal peak; any other shutdown keeps the flow until the firebox has cooled.

                            4e · Emergency shutdown and restart after a trip

                            A spurious trip at design rate with the crude kept flowing (HS-105B used as the demand); 1 min to diagnose (assumed), EMS reset, 120 s purge, relight on gas, TIC-101 back in AUTO from the outlet temperature it finds and ramped to 388 °C, then fuel oil readmitted by hand (PIC-112 in MAN) and put back in AUTO at 689 kPa.

                            5 · Load following: crude rate 175 → 218.75 m³/h

                            Lined out at 175 m³/h first; FIC-114 then ramped at the rate shown, with the draws (HCV-101/102), pumparound and steam flows and the fuel-oil pressure moved in proportion to the rate (the "rate-change recipe"). TIC-101 holds the outlet with fuel gas; window 3 h.

                            Control the result, not a sum of demands

                            6 · Crude switch: light → heavy crude

                            From design. "Step" is a tank switch; a blend changes the heavy fraction linearly over the time shown. TIC-101 and the column loops stay in AUTO.

                            7 · Storage sizing: V = F · t

                            Product made during a transition, or a stream that has nowhere to go during an outage, needs a tank. Pick a case from the runs above or type your own flow and time.

                            The 25 % margin covers unpumpable heel and a second event before the tank is worked off (assumed). Off-spec times are from the model runs; outage lengths are assumed.

                            Process reliability · atmospheric crude unit

                            Rev 0 · Issued for teaching. How often the unit stops making product, why, and what would make it stop less. Every model number comes from runs on private copies of the simulator (never the running one); generic failure rates and human response times are assumed and labelled so.

                            Production, not safety. This tab counts outages per year: heater trips, forced shutdowns and the hours of lost crude processing. Whether a safeguard works when it is needed (probability of failure on demand, risk reduction) is a different question with different numbers: see the LOPA tab. A design change can help one and hurt the other: a second trip sensor voted 1oo2 is safer and trips more often.
                            1 Definitions · 2 Availability vs reliability · 3 Weibull and the bathtub · 4 Structures · 5 Standby pumps here · 6 The unit as a series system · 7 Design for reliability · 8 Tube-skin life · 9 Inventory · 10 Maintenance strategies · 11 Pump life-cycle cost · 12 Fired-heater audit

                            1 · Definitions

                            2 · Availability is not reliability

                            A = MTTF/(MTTF + MTTR) tells how much of the time the unit can produce; R(t) = e−t/MTTF tells the chance of getting through a period with no outage. Compare a unit with many short trips against one with a rare long stop.

                            3 · Weibull lab and the bathtub curve

                            R(t) = exp[−(t/η)β], hazard h(t) = (β/η)(t/η)β−1. β < 1 infant mortality, β = 1 random, β > 1 wear-out. The dashed curve adds three Weibulls into the classic bathtub.

                            4 · Structures: series, parallel, standby, k-of-N

                            Series: every element must run (the ACU is mostly this). Parallel: all run, any one is enough (two air-cooler bays). Standby: the spare waits and must be switched in (P-1A/B … P-9A/B). k-of-N: k of N must work (3 × 50 % pumps are 2-of-3; a 2oo3 transmitter vote).

                            5 · The standby warning, applied to this unit

                            A standby pump only prevents an outage if it is running before the process notices. The formula N/λ assumes a perfect, instant switch. Pumps with spares here: P-1, P-2, P-3, P-5, P-6, P-7, P-8, P-9 A/B; no spare: P-10 (bottom pumparound) and P-4 (sour water). The fired heater cannot ride through a loss of pass flow: FSL-105A/B trip the fuel after 5 s below 40 m³/h. The model tells how long each loss takes to hurt (running pump tripped at design, nothing done), and by bisection the latest spare start that still avoids an outage (the switch window). Manual start assumed: median 4 min (alarm, walk, check, start), log-σ 0.7, 5 % fail to start. Auto-start assumed: median 5 s, log-σ 0.3, 3 % fail to start.

                            Outage criteria in the runs: heater trip (model EMS), V-1 bottoms level 99 % (residue backs into the flash zone) or V-4 level 99 % (liquid to the off-gas system) — the two level criteria are assumed shutdown points. "Product loss" adds off-spec or stopped products, a full stripper, a full sour-water boot or gas to flare.

                            Try it: start the spare after a delay (model run on a copy)

                            Pick a pump and a delay, then run (about a second).

                            6 · The unit as a series system

                            Any element that stops crude processing is in series. For each: generic all-modes failure rate λ (assumed) × the fraction of failures that stop the unit (from the model windows above, the voting logic, or assumed), and the time down per outage (repair if needed + restart). λsys = Σ λifi, MTTF = 8760/λsys h, R(1 yr) = e−λsys, unavailability = Σ λifi·downi/8760. Tick options to see their effect. The element list with the options now ticked is exported to other tabs as RL_EL.

                            Each option on its own

                            Reading it. The two charge-side pumps dominate because their windows (about a minute for P-1, a few seconds for P-2) are shorter than any manual start: the spare shortens the outage but does not prevent it. Auto-start is the single biggest lever; even then P-2's window is so short that a share of its trips still reaches the heater. Voting changes cut both ways: 2oo3 transmitters with a mid-value select cut spurious trips; a second flame scanner voted 1oo2 doubles them; separate trip transmitters cure the independence gap that LOPA cares about but add outages, because a control transmitter failing high now causes a real low flow that the separate switch correctly trips on. A spare for P-10 changes no outage count in the model (the unit runs on with reflux at its limit) but removes the degraded hours and their fuel.

                            7 · Design for reliability

                            PrincipleThis unit todayImprovement to study
                            Remove single points of failureP-10 (a third of the tower heat removal) and P-4 have no spare; one flame scanner; one transmitter per pass for control and tripSpare P-10, 2oo3 pass-flow transmitters, 2oo3 scanners
                            Make the spare fast enoughAll spares manual; P-1 window about 1 min, P-2 a few seconds (section 5)Auto-start on low discharge pressure for P-1 and P-2, tested on a schedule
                            Give the process time (surge, hold-up)V-1 bottoms buys about 17 min after a P-3 trip, V-4 about 15 min after P-6; the pass flows have no hold-upSize hold-up for the response time you can achieve; protect what cannot be given time
                            Avoid spurious tripsShared transmitters, 1oo1 voting, burn-out upscale TEs2oo3 with diagnostics; trip delay reviewed in LOPA, never just lengthened
                            Degrade gracefullyFuel oil base load + gas swing: losing either fuel does not stop the heater (model run); compressor loss goes to flareKeep both fuels in service; flare is a loss and an emission, not a solution
                            Fail-safe directionSDV-106/112 fail closed; FCV-105A/B fail open (assumed)Check every valve's failure position against the outage it causes
                            Maintainable on lineSpares with isolation; exchangers without a full by-pass on both sides cannot be cleaned on lineBypasses round E-1, E-4, E-5 so fouling can be cleaned without a stop
                            Monitor degradationPass ΔP (PI-105A/B), TI-1007A/B gap, exchanger outlet temperaturesTrend UA of each exchanger and the pass ΔP; see the Efficiency tab for the energy side

                            8 · Tube-skin life lab

                            Creep life of heater tubes falls steeply with temperature. Assumed here: life halves for every 15 °C hotter, 100 000 h at the design skin temperature. Because life responds exponentially, a scattered skin temperature consumes more life than a steady one at the same mean: E[2ΔT/15] = 2μ/15·exp[(σ ln2/15)²/2]. The model gives the skin at design, against COT and against coke.

                            Efficiency · atmospheric crude unit

                            Rev 0 · Issued for teaching. Where the energy of this unit goes and what it costs to waste it. Model numbers come from sweeps run offline on the unit's own model (design warm start, one change, one hour, mean of the last five minutes) or from runs on a private copy in the page; the running simulator is only read, never changed. Anything the model does not compute is a labelled calculation on assumed values.

                            1 Definition and priorities · 2 Chains multiply · 3 Heater efficiency · 4 Whole-unit energy · 5 Excess air · 6 Preheat fouling · 7 Crude temperature · 8 Pumparounds · 9 Stripping steam · 10 Fuel-saving options · 11 Throttling vs VSD · 12 Constraint pushing · 13 One live point · 14 KEV dashboard

                            1 · What efficiency means here, and where it ranks

                            Efficiency = useful output ÷ resource used: heat into the crude per unit of fuel, product value per unit of crude, hydraulic work per unit of electricity. It is pursued only inside the higher priorities:

                            2 · Chains multiply

                            3 · Heater H-1: direct and indirect efficiency

                            Direct (input–output): η = Qabsorbed by crude / Qfired, read live from the simulator. Indirect (losses): η = 1 − stack loss − casing loss − unburnt, where stack loss = ṁfluecp(Tstack − Tamb)/Qfired. The model has no flue gas, so the indirect side runs on the assumed O₂, stack temperature and casing loss below.

                            4 · Whole-unit energy: preheat and pumparound recovery

                            5 · Excess air and fuel

                            6 · Preheat fouling against fuel (model sweeps)

                            The exchanger fouling faults (E-1 up to −60 % UA, E-4 and E-5 up to −70 %) run at 0, 20 … 100 % severity.

                            7 · Crude inlet temperature against fuel (model sweep)

                            8 · Pumparound duty against heat recovery (model sweeps)

                            9 · Stripping steam: product quality against energy (model sweeps)

                            10 · Fuel-saving options sized for this unit

                            Savings at the design rate for 8400 operating hours per year (assumed). A model-run saving is the difference between two runs; a calculation uses the assumed stack values of section 3.

                            11 · Pump throttling against a variable-speed drive

                            A throttled pump makes the head of its curve and the control valve burns the excess; a VSD makes only the head the system needs plus a margin for control. Pump curves and system resistances are the model's own (dP = H₀n² − aF²).

                            12 · Constraint pushing

                            The closer the average runs to a limit, the more often it crosses it: P(exceed) = ½ erfc[(limit − set point)/(σ√2)]. The best set point balances the value of running closer against the cost of the crossings, and it moves toward the limit as σ shrinks.

                            13 · One live point on the model

                            Combine a fouled E-1, colder crude and new pumparound flows, then run 40 min on a private copy at design with the trips held out of reach (about two seconds).

                            14 · Key energy variables (live)

                            Read from the running simulator every half second; a red edge means worse than design by more than 2 %. Go to the Process tab, change something, and come back.

                            SOP · standard operating procedures of the crude unit

                            Rev 0 · Issued for teaching. Thirteen SOPs for the atmospheric crude unit, written around this simulator: every limit, trip setting, set point and EMS permissive in a step is read from the running page (alarm list, K, the design snapshot, the EMS logic and the model procedures), and the Safety, HAZOP, LOPA and Transition tab results are quoted where they exist. Values marked "assumed" are not in the design data.

                            1 What an SOP is · 2 Format · 3 Register · 4 Viewer · 5 Writing rules · 6 Life cycle

                            1 · What an SOP is, and which activities need one

                            A standard operating procedure is the written, approved way to do one operating task: what to do, in what order, by whom, what the plant should do in response, and why. It turns the design intent, the HAZOP and the safeguards into actions an operator can follow at 3 a.m. It is also the training standard: the OTS graded procedures check the same order and the same limits.

                            The US process safety management rule (OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119, paragraph (f)) requires written procedures for each operating phase below, with the operating limits, the safety and health considerations and the safety systems; paragraph (f)(4) adds the safe work practices. The last column shows which SOPs of this register cover each item; click a number to open it.

                            6 · Life cycle of an SOP

                            An SOP is never finished. It is reviewed whenever the plant, a limit or a chemical changes (management of change), after every incident or near miss it touches, and certified as current every year. Operators are trained on it and checked before they use it alone.
